Several system-level safety protocols and standards are emerging and available for guidance.2 The selection of relevant standards by the OMA will identify both the acceptable risk level and other supporting protocols and policies to be included in the AMD implementation program. 3.3.2 District-Level Safety Case Analysis The domain of an OMA encompasses the execution of a hazard analysis and risk assessment to determine necessary risk mitigations analogous to traffic warrant studies performed in analysis of traffic today. This is commonly known in associated domains as preparing a “safety case” for operations resulting in determination and enforcement of safe operating rules. Ultimately, the preparation of the safety case for the safety-critical junctions and operating zones within an AMD will come down to understanding the types of AV fleets that would be operating within the district and their various failure mechanisms, particularly with respect to mixed-use traffic conditions. Specific hazard analyses will address acceptable configuration and operational practice for AVs within the multimodal traffic of conventional human-operated vehicles, AV transit, and AV ride-hailing fleets—especially when the vehicles are interacting with pedestrians, bicyclists, and other active transportation modes. With the new technology and operational conditions of a district with multiple AV fleets in service, the OMA may also lead in any safety assessment resulting from the composite operations of multiple different AV fleets and the associated challenge of communicating and coordinating with multiple fleet operators. 3.3.3 Incident and Vehicle Failure Response Considerations Operations responsibility for an OMA would include the development of instructions and protocols for safe fallback conditions when a fleet AV’s ADS disengages or when similar AV system failures occur. At a minimum, such a protocol typically—at least during early deployments—brings the vehicle to a safe stop. Situations in which a vehicle reverts to a fallback condition can be as simple as exceeding the operational design domain limits of weather conditions (e.g., high winds or low visibility) or as complicated as a control system failure. Either case should be considered a failure in which a safe operating fallback protocol is required for fleet AVs as well as safety provisions for all pedestrians/bicyclists and human-operated vehicles in proximity to the vehicle(s) in fallback mode. Any given AV technology will have unique fallback behaviors in the case of an internal vehicle fault—determined and engineered by the technology provider.
